findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register - Annex B -Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Waste Recovery Plant contractor support £700k annually expires October 2026 during transition to new commercial contract.
findings.detail: Current contractor support of approximately £700k per year expires October 2026 as the facility transitions to a new commercial contract model. The new model includes risk apportionment and a target stoploss mechanism after 24 months to reduce revenue costs, but the register notes that market volatility and engineering challenges continue to drive up risk costing.
findings.matters: Contract transitions for critical infrastructure carry implementation risk, particularly for a facility with recent catastrophic failures. A lender would want assurance that the new commercial model reduces rather than increases the council's financial exposure.
findings.figures: Expiring support £700k annually; current disposal costs £7.8M pa; monthly contingency cost if unavailable ~£840k.
findings.quote: M1/M2 structure transition will ensure that there is a stoploss on revenue spend after 24 months. Market volatility and engineering challenges still driving risk costing.

findings.paper_title: Strategic Risk Register - Annex B -Strategic Risk Register
findings.headline: Waste Recovery Plant experienced catastrophic failure in October 2025, less than a year before this register.
findings.detail: The facility had a catastrophic boiler failure in October 2025, its second such failure in three years (previous failure October 2022). Each failure made the plant unable to carry out thermal treatment and energy export for four months. If the plant becomes unavailable again, the council must cover approximately £840k monthly in waste disposal contingency costs and related expenses.
findings.matters: Lenders need assurance that critical council infrastructure is reliable. Recent catastrophic failure of a key waste disposal asset indicates vulnerability, and each outage forces significant contingency spending at scale.
findings.figures: Monthly unavailability cost ~£840k. Disposal costs £7.8M pa, staff costs £300k pa, insurances £1.1M pa, NNDR £800k pa. Both failures resulted in 4 months of unavailability.
findings.quote: A catastrophic boiler failure occurred in October 2022 and October 2025. Both resulted in thermal treatment and energy export being unavailable) for 4 months.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: Garage portfolio rationalization strategy reducing asset base with reliance on capital receipts from disposals for reinvestment
findings.detail: Milton Keynes is rationalizing its garage estate to 1,200–1,600 retained units with improved occupancy, while disposing of surplus garages through sale, demolition or repurposing. Capital receipts from these disposals will partially fund reinvestment in maintenance and improvements to retained stock.
findings.matters: Dependency on capital receipts from asset disposals creates funding volatility; it also indicates the council's capital programme relies on asset sales rather than external funding, and suggests historical asset underutilization.
findings.figures: 1,200–1,600 garages to be retained; estimated capital receipts from surplus garage sales (amount unspecified)
findings.quote: The report recommends rationalising the Council's garage estate to create a smaller, financially sustainable portfolio. Around 1,200–1,600 garages would be retained and improved to achieve occupancy and generate annual income. Poorly performing or surplus garages would be repurposed, demolished or sold, generating estimated capital receipts.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: Unforeseen structural defects at River Valley Community Centre required supplementary capital funding of £0.045m
findings.detail: River Valley Community Centre required additional capital funding of £0.045m from the Health & Safety programme following detailed surveys and structural investigations that identified unforeseen defects and site constraints not apparent when the initial budget was established.
findings.matters: Cost overruns from unforeseen defects discovered during project delivery indicate potential estimation weaknesses and signal risk of further supplementary funding being required on other schemes.
findings.figures: £0.045m additional funding from Health & Safety fund
findings.quote: The additional funding requirement has arisen following detailed surveys, structural investigations, and contractor assessments which identified unforeseen defects and site constraints not evident when the initial budget allocation was established.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: Capital equipment replacement brought forward due to rising market prices; Housing Infrastructure Fund expanded to cover construction cost inflation
findings.detail: The council is accelerating £0.500m of IT capital funding into 2026/27 to replace 1,650 laptops based on latest market prices that have risen since the original budget. Additionally, Homes England increased the Housing Infrastructure Fund grant by £50m specifically recognising that construction cost inflation had impacted the Milton Keynes East development delivery timescale.
findings.matters: Cost inflation pressures on capital equipment and construction signal rising capital delivery costs and can erode budget headroom if original allocations become insufficient for planned projects.
findings.figures: £0.500m brought forward for IT replacement (1,650 devices); £50m additional HIF funding attributable to construction cost inflation
findings.quote: Approval is sought to bring forward £0.500m of funding from later years into 2026/27 to enable the planned replacement of 1,650 laptop devices, based on the latest market prices.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex C - Capital Revisions
findings.headline: Environmental remediation requirement of £0.544m at household waste facility to address contamination risks
findings.detail: New Bradwell Household Waste Recycling Centre requires £0.544m in targeted remediation works to address contamination risks and support continued safe operation. The council prioritised this spending to avoid the higher costs of full remediation, closure or mothballing, and to reduce environmental and regulatory risks while retaining a strategic waste asset.
findings.matters: Environmental liabilities and remediation costs represent real balance-sheet impacts and regulatory risk that lenders assess when evaluating council creditworthiness.
findings.figures: £0.544m capital cost; funded through revenue contributions
findings.quote: The project seeks approval for targeted remediation works at the New Bradwell Household Waste Recycling Centre to address contamination risks and support the site's continued safe operation. The estimated capital cost is £0.544m, funded through revenue contributions, subject to approval. The project will help retain a strategic waste asset, reduce environmental and regulatory risks, support future lease income, and avoid the higher costs associated with full remediation, closure or mothballing.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: £15m CCLA property fund investment has fallen to £13.819m; unrealised loss of £1.181m with no exit plan
findings.detail: Council invested £15m in CCLA pooled property fund (£10m March 2015, £5m February 2016). Holding fell £0.167m this quarter alone. Total unrealised loss now £1.181m. Document states 'we have no immediate plans to liquidate this investment,' indicating bet on property market recovery.
findings.matters: Loss exposes council to property market risk; size of loss growing; continued hold strategy depends on market conditions stabilising
findings.figures: £13.819m current value, £15.0m invested, £1.181m total unrealised loss, £0.167m Q1 loss
findings.quote: On 30th June 2026, our holdings stood at £13.819m against opening balance of £13.986m on 1st April 2026, representing a fair value loss so far this year of £0.167m and an overall unrealised loss of £1.181m against the £15.0m total cash deposited.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: £41.5m of HRA internal debt from General Fund matures within six months; £30m of it at elevated 4.48% rate
findings.detail: £11.5m loan at 1.75% matures 26/02/2027; £30.0m loan at 4.48% matures 19/03/2027. These internal loans must be refinanced, renewed or repaid. The £30m is a new 1-year loan agreed March 2026 at current high rates.
findings.matters: Creates near-term refinancing risk; if General Fund cannot renew, HRA must access external market or service costs will spike; £30m at 4.48% signals rate-lock risk if rates fall

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Management Update
findings.headline: HRA approaching point of requiring additional external borrowing; forecast £70m new loans to fund capital programme
findings.detail: HRA capital programme cannot be funded from reserves and cash flow. Currently receiving £80m internal loans from General Fund (£11.5m due Feb 2027, £30m due Mar 2027). Forecast outturn assumes £70m new external borrowing; further internal loans may be considered. HRA external debt currently £196.360m.
findings.matters: Signals weakening HRA financial resilience and rising debt burden; capacity to serve housing stock depends on sustained external/internal funding
findings.figures: £70m new external loans forecast, £80.0m internal loans outstanding, £196.360m current HRA external debt, £11.5m and £30.0m maturing Feb-Mar 2027
findings.quote: The HRA is approaching a point of requiring additional funding to meet its business plan capital objectives (subject to slippage). The HRA forecast outturn figures shown above assumes £70m funded by new external loans, but further internal loans may be considered.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex B - General Fund
findings.headline: High Needs Block expected into deficit in 2026/27 with unclear impact on general fund budget
findings.detail: The council notes High Needs Block (education funding for high-cost pupils) is expected to go into deficit in 2026/27. Impact on general fund is unclear pending government announcements on whether any financial support will be provided or whether council must absorb the shortfall from general resources.
findings.matters: High Needs deficits often become general fund pressures. Council does not currently know what its liability will be, creating budget uncertainty.
findings.figures: Deficit expected 2026/27; amount unspecified
findings.quote: High Needs Block - is expected to go into Deficit in 2026/27 - Impact on GF Budget is currently unclear as we await Government announcements on whether there will be any financial support.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex B - General Fund
findings.headline: National Living Wage inflation risk: if actual increase is 5% rather than budgeted 3.7%, adds £1.9m pressure
findings.detail: Social care provider contracts are indexed to National Living Wage and Foundation Living Wage. The MTFO assumes midrange increase of 3.7%. If actual increases follow the high-range position of 5%, this adds £1.9m pressure in 2027/28 alone. The actual figure will not be confirmed until later in the financial year, creating budget uncertainty.
findings.matters: Social care is a major cost; wage inflation is outside council control and legislatively mandated. This is genuine inflation risk compounded by late confirmation of rates.
findings.figures: £1.9m if 5% realised versus 3.7% assumed; £26.2m total social care inflation over MTFO
findings.quote: There is a risk that the 2027/28 assumptions on FLW/NLW will vary from the actual increase which will not be published until later in the financial year. The current forecast position includes the midrange of the expected increase in NLW/FLW 3.7%. If the actual increase reflects the high range position on 5% could lead to a pressure of £1.9m.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex B - General Fund
findings.headline: Council must identify £3.840m additional savings by 2031 through unspecified transformation programme business cases
findings.detail: The MTFO forecasts cumulative gap of £3.840m over four years. The council has identified £12.572m in savings but needs a further £3.840m. These are to come from the 'Changing Because We Have To' programme focused on productivity and service redesign. However, the detailed business cases for the additional savings are not yet available and will be brought forward only after the draft budget publication.
findings.matters: Budget balance is dependent on delivery of a transformation programme with unspecified details. Such programmes frequently deliver less than planned or take longer to realise benefits.
findings.figures: £3.840m cumulative gap; £12.572m savings identified; need £3.840m more
findings.quote: Based on the updated financial projection further savings of £3.840m are needed by 31/3/2031. Directors are currently developing the detailed savings proposals and service reviews that have addressed budget gap. The business cases for these will be brought forward following the publication of the draft budget.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex B - General Fund
findings.headline: New waste recovery park contract adds £2.4m ongoing cost pressure dependent on market prices for energy and recyclate
findings.detail: The MKWRP procurement concluded with contract costs now £0.5m higher than estimated. This £2.4m is included as base budget pressure from 2027/28. Actual net costs will depend on tonnage volumes, recyclate market prices, energy prices, and plant running costs, all outside council control. The new contractor has a discovery period to identify efficiencies.
findings.matters: This is a substantial new variable cost exposure with significant market price volatility. Energy and commodities markets are unpredictable; council has already revised cost forecast once.
findings.figures: £0.5m cost increase from initial projection; £2.4m base budget pressure from 2027/28; waste contract £42m in 2026/27
findings.quote: Following the conclusion of the tender and extension of the current contractor we now expect costs to be about £0.500m higher than previously projected and we have included this £2.400m as a base budget pressure from 2027/28.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex B - General Fund
findings.headline: Council assumes 16% of looked-after children in residential care can be reduced to 12% by 2028/29 to manage £4.272m pressure
findings.detail: Milton Keynes has significantly higher proportion of children in expensive residential placements compared to other councils. The MTFO depends on management actions reducing this to average levels through moving children to lower-cost placements and expanding in-house foster care. The council explicitly flags in its risks section that if these plans do not materialise, there is a significant financial risk to the budget.
findings.matters: This is a multi-million pound assumption underpinning the budget. Demand-led social care costs are hard to control; if placement reduction targets slip, the council faces immediate unbudgeted pressure.
findings.figures: Currently 16% of LAC in residential settings; target 12% by 2028/29; £4.272m saving in 2027/28
findings.quote: The cohort of residential placements as a % of the overall looked after children population is significantly higher than in previous years and compared to other Local Authorities. Currently 16% of LAC are placed in external residential settings. The MTFP assumes that MKCC will reduce this in line with the LA average of 12%.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex B - Reserves
findings.headline: Reserves forecast to decline by £21.566m in 2026-27, driven by tariff and waste asset drawdowns
findings.detail: Milton Keynes' Q1 2026-27 forecast projects total reserves will fall from £258.238m to £236.672m by year-end (a net 8% reduction). The drawdown is primarily due to tariff reserve reduction of £4.156m, waste asset renewal fund drawdown of £3.571m, and change reserves drawdown of £1.307m. The General Fund Balance is forecast to remain static at £34.677m.
findings.matters: For a lender assessing creditworthiness, reserve depletion is a material financial resilience indicator. An 8% year-on-year decline in reserves requires explanation—whether it reflects structural deficit requiring sustained drawdown, or planned allocation to capital and programme costs. The static General Fund Balance alongside broader reserve decline suggests targeted reserve usage, but the sustainability of this position depends on whether the decline is recurring.
findings.figures: Opening balance £258.238m, closing balance £236.672m (£21.566m decline); tariff reserve £4.156m, waste asset renewals £3.571m, change reserves £1.307m; General Fund Balance stable at £34.677m
findings.quote: Opening Balance on reserves (258.238) ... Closing Balance on Reserves (236.672)

findings.headline: Homelessness Prevention Duty risk escalated for deep audit review
findings.detail: The Audit Committee has ordered a special task group deep dive into Strategic Risk SR06 (Homelessness Prevention Duty), separate from routine quarterly monitoring. The escalation from standard risk oversight suggests this area is not being managed satisfactorily within normal controls.
findings.matters: Failure to meet statutory homelessness prevention duties exposes the council to legal liability and reputational damage; an audit escalation signals potential resource or capacity shortfalls that could affect service delivery and finances.
findings.figures: Not provided in this paper.
findings.quote: At the meeting in July 2026, Audit Committee determined to set up a task group to undertake a deep dive on the risk SR06 – Homelessness Prevention Duty. This is to be scheduled.

findings.headline: HRA exposed to interest rate risk from significant borrowing with potential capital needs on horizon
findings.detail: While the Housing Revenue Account business plan is currently balanced, the paper flags that it 'remains exposed to interest rate risk due to the level of borrowing required to finance existing schemes and refinance existing borrowing'. Stock condition surveys may also identify additional investment needs that would increase capital expenditure.
findings.matters: Interest rate rises could materially impact HRA viability and potentially require General Fund subsidy, and unplanned capital needs would add to the capital funding gap.
findings.figures: Borrowing level and interest cover ratio thresholds not specified; refinancing risk explicitly flagged
findings.quote: The HRA remains exposed to interest rate risk due to the level of borrowing required to finance existing schemes and refinance existing borrowing. This could place additional pressure on the HRA Business Plan.

findings.headline: Capital programme fully committed with unquantified funding gap requiring difficult choices
findings.detail: The council has allocated all currently available resources to the capital programme through 2032. In the December budget review they will present 'an updated view on the potential funding gap and the choices that will need to be made between 2027/28 and 2031/32', indicating that new capital investment will require prioritisation or funding solutions.
findings.matters: A capital programme with no headroom limits the council's ability to invest in infrastructure, service modernisation, and regeneration plans mentioned in their Council Plan.
findings.figures: Not quantified in this paper; details will be in December 2026 Draft Budget and Capital Programme report
findings.quote: The Council has committed all currently available resources to finance the existing capital programme... this will include an updated view on the potential funding gap and the choices that will need to be made between 2027/28 and 2031/32.

findings.headline: Structural budget gap grows to £3.840m by 2030/31 with savings plan not yet finalised
findings.detail: The medium term forecast shows Milton Keynes moving from a small £0.117m surplus in 2027/28 to cumulative gaps of £4.078m (2028/29), £1.114m (2029/30), and £3.840m (2030/31). The council acknowledges 'a number of risks within the General Fund budget, together with areas that require further review' that have been excluded from the forecast.
findings.matters: A structural gap of this scale requires major spending reductions or new revenue sources, and the council has not yet identified sufficient detailed savings proposals to close it.
findings.figures: Cumulative gap: £0.117m surplus 2027/28; £4.078m deficit 2028/29; £1.114m deficit 2029/30; £3.840m deficit 2030/31
findings.quote: The latest forecast shows a base budget funding gap of £3.840m by 2030/31, with a surplus of (£0.117m) in 2027/28. However, there remain a number of risks within the General Fund budget, together with areas that require further review and have therefore not been included in the current forecast.

findings.headline: High needs budget faces likely deficit in 2027/28 after exhausting all reserves
findings.detail: The council used all remaining brought forward surplus to balance the 2026/27 high needs budget. The paper explicitly states there is a risk of the block going into deficit in-year if there is any overspend, making it 'therefore likely we may start the 2027/28 financial year in a deficit.' A full review of high needs spending is underway but no solution is yet identified.
findings.matters: A high needs deficit that extends into the General Fund directly threatens financial stability and could require emergency General Fund subsidy to service schooling obligations.
findings.figures: 2026/27 budget balanced using all remaining brought forward surplus; 2027/28 start likely to be in deficit; national high needs deficit estimated at £5 billion across councils
findings.quote: The 2026/27 budget has been balanced by using all the remaining brought forward surplus therefore there is a chance that the block will go into a deficit during the 2026/27 if there were to be any in year overspend. It is therefore likely we may start the 2027/28 financial year in a deficit.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: Reema demolition project discovers asbestos requiring removal during Phase 1, affecting schedule and contingency
findings.detail: During Phase 1 of the R&M Reema demolition project, asbestos has been identified in building blocks requiring removal before works can proceed. Phase 1 is due to complete in September, with future phases to be confirmed once initial asbestos removal is complete.
findings.matters: Asbestos remediation during demolition is an unforeseen cost driver that cannot be precisely estimated until survey and removal assessment is complete; this is a routine but material risk in building demolition projects that can consume contingency budgets.
findings.figures: R&M Reema Demolition Phase 1 forecast £1.31m; Phase 2-3 costs unconfirmed pending asbestos assessment
findings.quote: Contractor appointed and started on site May. Asbestos identified in blocks, to be removed, Phase 1 to be completed Sept. Future phases to be confirmed

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: Bradwell Windmill cultural project paused following tender receipt due to costs exceeding budget
findings.detail: Tenders for works to Bradwell Windmill have been received but costs exceed the available budget of £304k. The project is now paused pending council review of options and next steps, with the project timeline requiring extension to be confirmed.
findings.matters: An unresolved cost overrun on a discretionary project means either the original budget was significantly underestimated or scope has grown; project pause indicates no agreed path forward yet, risking further delay or abandonment.
findings.figures: Budget £304,350; costs quoted in tender exceed this; project Amber status
findings.quote: Tenders to deliver required work received, however cost in excess of current budget, project paused as options and next steps reviewed, project timeline will require extension, to be confirmed.

findings.paper_title: Q1 2026-27 Forecast Outturn Report - Annex D - Capital Monitoring
findings.headline: MK East HIF social infrastructure project overshooting by £400,000 due to unexpected utility connection costs
findings.detail: The £29.2m HIF social infrastructure project is forecast to overspend by £400,000 because lengthy and costly measures were required to provide power, water and drainage in lieu of permanent utility connections. The council has identified tariff funding to cover the overspend, with recommissioning partly completed and forecast including assumed final account contract costs.
findings.matters: Material project overspend (1.4% on a £29.2m scheme) reveals site cost surprises either missed at tender stage or caused by changed requirements; reliance on tariff funding means overspend recovery depends on developer contributions materialising as assumed.
findings.figures: Total scheme forecast £29.6m; capital budget £29.2m; forecast overspend £400,000
findings.quote: Overspend due to lengthy measures to provide power/water/drainage in lieu of permanent connections. Recommissioning partly completed; forecast includes assumed final account contract costs, Tariff funding identified for overspend.

findings.paper_title: Medium Term Financial Outlook 2027/28 to 2030/31 - Annex A - Economic Update
findings.headline: Inflationary pressure identified as MKCC's most substantial financial challenge
findings.detail: The council identifies inflationary pressure from international economic trends as its most substantial financial challenge for the 2027/28 MTFO period. CPI is forecast to rise to 3.2% by end of 2026/27 before stabilizing to 1.7% in 2027/28, and the National Living Wage has risen 4.1% to £12.71.
findings.matters: Inflation directly increases council payroll, service delivery, and utility costs; a lender needs to understand what the council sees as its primary financial risk.
findings.figures: CPI 2.6% June 2026, forecast 3.2% end of 2026/27, then 1.7% end of 2027/28. National Living Wage up 4.1% to £12.71.
findings.quote: For MKCC, this risk, particularly in relation to inflationary pressure, represents the most substantial financial challenge in the 2027/28 MTFO period.

findings.headline: Interest rate risk on borrowing: elevated rates could increase forecast costs
findings.detail: The council notes explicit risk that interest rates may remain elevated or increase further during 2026/27, resulting in higher borrowing costs than currently forecast. This is flagged separately from the general forecast position.
findings.matters: Council has exposure to rising interest rates on its borrowing; this is a documented risk that could reduce the forecast underspend if rates exceed assumptions.
findings.figures: No amount quantified; risk flagged as 'continued elevation or increase'
findings.quote: There is however, the risk that later in 2026/27 interest rates continue to be elevated or even increase further, resulting in higher borrowing costs.

findings.headline: Savings delivery only 45% complete at Q1; remainder must be achieved to hit outturn forecast
findings.detail: The council approved £9.982m of savings (including £0.530m carried forward from 2025/26). Only £4.184m has been achieved to date (42%), with £9.356m (94%) forecast to be achieved in-year. A further £0.530m is expected to slip to 2027/28 and £0.096m is marked as undeliverable, requiring review for 2027/28 planning.
findings.matters: The reported underspend depends on delivering savings that are currently less than halfway achieved; failure to deliver the forecast amount would erase the underspend and move into overspend territory.
findings.figures: £4.184m achieved to date of £9.356m forecast (42%); £0.530m to slip; £0.096m undeliverable
findings.quote: £9.356m of savings built into the 2026/27 budget are forecast to be achieved in year. £4.184m has been achieved to date but the remainder of the savings need to be delivered to ensure that the reported outturn position is as reported.

findings.headline: HRA grant recovery at risk: SHDF lodgement deadline passed without confirmation of extension
findings.detail: Mears is continuing to lodge claims under the Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund (SHDF) but the submission deadline has passed. The council is seeking clarification on whether the deadline will be extended. Without an extension, the council will be unable to recover the full amount of grant eligible on completed works.
findings.matters: The HRA's ability to recover grant funding on completed capital works is now uncertain after the deadline; this affects the financing plan for housing investment.
findings.figures: Amount at risk not quantified in this extract
findings.quote: SHDF lodgements – At the end of Period 3 Mears are continuing to lodge claims. The deadline has passed and we are seeking clarification as to whether this will be extended further. Without an extension the council will be unable to recover the full amount of grant eligible on completed works.

findings.headline: Three significant debts written off including £362k casino operator in administration
findings.detail: The council is writing off three debts exceeding the £50k threshold for Cabinet approval. These include a £362,607 commercial debt from a former casino provider that has entered administration; and business rates debts of £167,864 (Dough & Co, in liquidation) and £55,961 (Say Estates, in liquidation). Total write-offs: £586,432.
findings.matters: Large debt write-offs indicate either failed commercial relationships or revenue loss from business insolvencies; the casino debt is particularly significant.
findings.figures: £362,607 commercial; £167,864 business rates; £55,961 business rates; total £586,432
findings.quote: A commercial debt of £362,607 is recommended for write-off following confirmation that the former casino provider company has entered administration... Dough&Co Milton Keynes Ltd Jul 24 – Mar 25 £167,864 In Liquidation... Say Estates Ltd Jan 22 – Feb 26 £55,961 In Liquidation

findings.headline: Public Health reserve being drawn down by 32% in single year
findings.detail: The council is drawing £1.074m from the Public Health reserve during 2026/27 to support one-off initiatives approved in the budget. This reduces the reserve from £3.379m to £2.305m. The service itself is forecasting in-line with budget.
findings.matters: A large one-time drawdown (32% of the reserve in one year) reduces the cushion available for future Public Health pressures or one-off costs.
findings.figures: £1.074m drawdown; reserve falls from £3.379m to £2.305m
findings.quote: Public Health is forecasting a £1.074m drawdown from the Public Health Reserve during 2026/27, reducing the reserve balance from £3.379m at 31 March 2026 to £2.305m at 31 March 2027.

findings.headline: Major capital scheme (HIF infrastructure) overrunning; requires additional tariff funding
findings.detail: The MK East HIF-funded social infrastructure project had a total project overspend of £1.1m forecast at Q3 2025/26. By year-end, £0.7m had been spent with a further £0.4m now forecast in 2026/27. The overspend stems from prolonged temporary power, water and drainage arrangements. The council must identify additional funding from future tariff receipts (developer contributions).
findings.matters: A scheme generating investment-linked infrastructure is overrunning its budget and requires the council to fund the gap from developer tariff income, constraining availability for other schemes.
findings.figures: £0.400m overspend in 2026/27; £1.100m total project overspend
findings.quote: The overspend is mainly due to the prolonged use of temporary power, water and drainage arrangements while permanent connections are put in place. Additional funding will need to be identified and approved from future tariff receipts.

findings.headline: Waste facility costs exceed budget in first year under council control
findings.detail: Milton Keynes took control of the MKWRP waste facility on 1 April 2026. Early costs in April and May are running higher than the approved budget. The council has made a £2m contingency provision but continues to flag it as a significant risk to the general fund.
findings.matters: A major operational facility that the council inherited at known cost is already overrunning; the budget risk is flagged explicitly in the risk register as something requiring 'close monitoring' through the year.
findings.figures: £2m provision in contingency; costs higher than budget based on April and May actuals
findings.quote: Since April 2026 MKCC is responsible for all running costs and repairs at MKWRP. Initial estimates based on April and May, are reporting costs higher than budget, and whilst we have made a provision of £2m to be met from contingency, MKWRP remains a significant risk to the general fund budget.

findings.paper_title: Milton Keynes City Council - External Audit plan 2025-26 - Draft
findings.headline: Pension surplus model re-basing from triennial valuation could produce corrections to DBO and change contribution obligations
findings.detail: The 31 March 2025 Triennial Valuation will trigger re-basing of Milton Keynes's actuarial models, incorporating actual experience since 2022. This could result in corrections to the Defined Benefit Obligation and asset valuations, and updates to contribution payable. Recent market conditions have moved more councils into pension surplus, which carries complex accounting recognition rules and could affect the asset ceiling assessment.
findings.matters: Pension liability and contribution obligations are material balance-sheet and cash-flow items for any lender assessing council financial stability. A revaluation could reveal hidden liabilities or surpluses that affect solvency.
findings.figures: Triennial valuation as at 31 March 2025
findings.quote: The actuary will take account of the results of the new Triennial Valuation as at 31 March 2025 for accounting at 31 March 2026. This means re-basing their estimate models to allow for actual experience since 2022, which could result in corrections to the DBO and asset valuations this year. It also updates the contributions payable, which could have an impact on the assessment of the asset ceiling applying to the Council.

findings.paper_title: Milton Keynes City Council - External Audit plan 2025-26 - Draft
findings.headline: £119m investment property portfolio, almost entirely farmland held for development, carries fair value risk
findings.detail: The council's investment property is recorded at £119m and is primarily farmland held for development. There is a significant audit risk that these properties may not be held at fair value as required by accounting standards. KPMG will use its own valuation specialists to review the methodology and challenge key assumptions in the council's valuers' report.
findings.matters: A lender needs to understand the true economic value of this large balance-sheet asset; development farmland is illiquid and market-dependent, and any correction to fair value could be material to the council's financial position.
findings.quote: The fair value of investment properties recorded in the signed 24/25 financial statements was £119m. Almost all of this portfolio relates to farmland held for development.

findings.headline: HRA Social Housing Decarbonisation Fund Wave 2: £9.3m grant clawback due to reduced delivery
findings.detail: The SHDF Wave 2 programme was intended to improve 1,676 homes to EPC C but completed only 1,217 due to access difficulties, right-to-buy legislation changes mid-project, and uncovered stock condition issues. As a result, £9.3m of grant must be returned, funded through increased Revenue Contribution to Capital (RCCO) of £8.006m.
findings.matters: This shows capital programme delivery challenges and grant dependency risk. The council is using revenue to cover failed capital delivery, reducing revenue headroom.
findings.figures: 1,217 homes completed vs 1,676 funded; £9.3m grant clawback; £8.006m additional RCCO (total RCCO £12.053m)
findings.quote: The Council will need to return £9.3m grant from this project as a result of the reduced delivery programme... The additional RCCO will be used to refinance some of these costs, enabling repayment of the grant to the Government.

findings.headline: General Fund working balance only £2.215m above minimum, down by movements in-year
findings.detail: Current General Fund working balance is £34.677m against a minimum recommended level. This provides only £2.215m headroom. The paper proposes to add £2m to the Collection Fund reserve to manage NNDR volatility, which further pressures the general fund.
findings.matters: The council's liquidity buffer is tight and under pressure from collection fund deficits, contingency depletion, and ongoing demand pressures. There is limited room for further shocks.
findings.figures: General Fund balance £34.677m; minimum recommended unspecified but headroom £2.215m; proposed £2m addition to Collection Fund reserve
findings.quote: The current General Fund working balance is £34.677m, which provides headroom of £2.215m above than the minimum recommended level, providing a small buffer for unplanned expenditure.

findings.headline: Corporate contingency depleted by £4.1m for Waste Recovery Park catastrophic event, leaving only £1.5m
findings.detail: In October 2025 both steam drums at Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park failed, taking the Advanced Thermal Treatment plant offline until 18 January 2026. This was classified as a catastrophic event under contract and cost £4.1m in contingency funding. Of a £5.6m contingency, £1.5m now remains.
findings.matters: This shows the council is exposed to operational incidents at major facilities and has limited liquidity to absorb future shocks. The contingency is now at risk level.
findings.figures: £4.1m used from £5.6m contingency; £1.5m remaining; plant offline October 2025 to 18 January 2026
findings.quote: In 2025/26, the corporate contingency totalled £5.6m. Of this, £4.1m was used to fund a 'catastrophic event' at the Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park (MKWRP) in October 2025, when both steam drums were taken offline due to leaks.

findings.headline: Adult Social Care Autism and Learning Disabilities: demand and complexity outpacing budget
findings.detail: Autism overspent by £1.199m with 155 placements against 105 budgeted; Learning Disabilities overspent by £1.583m with 555 placements against 530 budgeted. Both driven by higher-than-budget numbers and lower client contribution income. These are underspends elsewhere masking underlying pressure.
findings.matters: These are ringfenced growth areas in ASC where demand and complexity are rising consistently and budgeted numbers are proving inadequate. The underspends in Assessment/Review (£2.639m) and Commissioning (£2.921m) may not be sustainable.
findings.figures: Autism: 155 placements vs 105 budget, £1.199m overspend; Learning Disabilities: 555 placements vs 530 budget, £1.583m overspend
findings.quote: Autism £1.199m (£1.029m in P9) Overspend due to a higher-than-budgeted number of care packages and lower client contribution income. There are currently 155 placements against a budget of 105 across direct payments, supported living and external home care.

findings.headline: Business Rates Collection Fund deficit of £6.230m: structural factors, not temporary
findings.detail: The deficit reflects: growth assumptions in the NNDR1 not materializing; rateable value changes and deletions on major properties; Section 26a restructurings (mandatory debt relief); higher empty properties; increased insolvencies; and a £12.549m increase in appeals provision due to higher settlements, outstanding cases rising significantly, and challenges to the 2023 valuation list deadline. MKCC's share is £10.2m.
findings.matters: This is not a one-year variance but multiple structural factors compressing the business rate base: growth stalling, retail pressure, and appeals risk that will likely persist into 2026/27.
findings.figures: £6.230m total deficit; MKCC share £10.2m; appeals provision increased £12.549m; gross rates yield £16m lower than NNDR1 forecast
findings.quote: The gross rates yield at the end of 2025/26 was £16m lower than anticipated in the 2025/26 NNDR1 return. This reduction was primarily due to the growth assumed in the NNDR1 not materialising during the year. Further reductions arose from a number of rateable value changes, including deletions and amendments affecting some large properties such as supermarkets.

findings.headline: Children's external residential placements £8.435m overspend, demand rising despite LAC reduction
findings.detail: 71 high-cost external residential placements in March against a budget of 48, costing £0.395m average per year. Despite the number of LAC falling, a greater proportion are now in residential placements rather than IFA (Independent Foster Agency), suggesting increasing complexity and cost per child.
findings.matters: This is a structural cost driver that the council cannot control through placement type — the children requiring these placements are growing and expensive, and budgeted numbers are now clearly unachievable.
findings.figures: 71 actual vs 48 budgeted placements; £0.395m average cost per placement; £8.435m outturn overspend (£8.623m P9)
findings.quote: As previously forecast the key pressure in this budget relates to the Increasing number of high-cost external residential placements required for our most complex children. There were 71 high-cost external residential placements in March, 2 mother and baby placements and 2 placements at Fenny House. This was against a budget of 48.

findings.headline: DSG Higher Needs Block heading into deficit in 2026/27
findings.detail: The Higher Needs block overspent by £1.864m in 2025/26, driven by independent school placements (£1.665m) and college top-up funding (£0.733m) as demand and complexity increased. The carry-forward balance has reduced to £1.239m. Based on forecast demand, the block will go into deficit next year.
findings.matters: A ring-fenced DSG deficit cannot be covered by general fund and locks the council into a structural budget problem that requires government intervention or service redesign.
findings.figures: £1.864m overspend; carry-forward £1.239m (down from £3.103m budgeted); High Needs allocation £65.677m
findings.quote: The high needs block continues to be under significant pressure and based on forecast demand it is expected that the block will go into deficit in 2026/27.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA debt service consumes 33.35% of net revenue; material constraint on service flexibility as borrowing requirement grows
findings.detail: The ratio of financing costs to net revenue for the HRA stands at 33.35%, down slightly from working assumptions but still consuming a third of HRA income. The council notes the HRA 'has less ability to utilise internal borrowing and typically benefits most from long-term funding certainty' — a constraint that tightens as debt grows towards the £121m three-year target.
findings.matters: At 33%+ of revenue, debt service consumes a high proportion of HRA funding, limiting flexibility to absorb cost pressures or invest in housing stock beyond minimum maintenance.
findings.figures: HRA financing cost ratio: 33.35% of net revenue; General Fund for comparison: 3.98%
findings.quote: Ratio of financing costs to net revenue streams: HRA 36.69 [indicator set] 33.35% [outturn]; HRA has less ability to utilise internal borrowing and typically benefits most from long-term funding certainty over short-term savings

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA reserves drawn down to suppress 2025/26 borrowing; £19m of minimum balances, capital and debt financing reserves used
findings.detail: To hold 2025/26 HRA borrowing at £30m instead of the £49m gross requirement, the council applied £19m of HRA minimum balance, capital reserve and debt financing reserve. This leaves less financial buffer for future shocks and constrains ability to delay borrowing again if markets move.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion reduces the council's ability to manage volatility and limits discretion in future treasury decisions. The document notes internal borrowing sustainability depends on 'planned use of reserves and cash-backed balances'.
findings.figures: £19m of reserves applied; gross HRA requirement £49m reduced to net requirement £30m
findings.quote: Certain balances and reserves such as the HRA minimum balance, Capital reserve and Debt Financing reserve are kept cash-backed, and these balances of £19m were applied to suppress the 2025/26 HRA borrowing need to a net requirement of £30m.

findings.paper_title: Quarter 4 2025/26 Outturn Report - Annex G - Treasury Outturn 2025-26
findings.headline: HRA borrowing accelerated after market shift: first new external debt in years, triggered by unexpected rate rises
findings.detail: The council had delayed HRA borrowing expecting rate reductions through 2026, but the Middle East conflict in March 2026 reversed that. They now took a £30m internal loan to the HRA (from General Fund) at 4.48%, and face a £121m cumulative borrowing requirement over three years (£49m, £40m, £32m). This marks a strategic pivot from cash-suppression to active debt raising.
findings.matters: A council forced to accelerate borrowing due to unforeseen market moves signals strategy execution risk and reduced flexibility to respond to future shocks.
findings.figures: £30m internal loan (March 2026); £121m cumulative HRA borrowing requirement over 2025/26 to 2027/28; 4.48% rate
findings.quote: So far, we have delayed raising new HRA borrowing through enhanced cash monitoring and to avoid locking in high cost of interest when forecasts predicted steady rate reductions over the next two years. Indeed, borrowing rates had begun to steadily fall since December 2025 until the conflict in the Middle East had a significant effect on financial markets, with borrowing rates rising dramatically

findings.headline: Pension scheme has moved into surplus with complex asset ceiling accounting required
findings.detail: The auditors note that recent market conditions have seen councils moving into pension fund surplus positions. Milton Keynes appears to be in this position. The auditors required an additional disclosure on asset ceiling reconciliation per IAS 19.40(a)(iii) to ensure transparency, indicating the council's initial disclosures were incomplete on this complex area.
findings.matters: Pension surplus positions are rare and create complex accounting questions about asset ceiling recognition that directly affect reported reserves and borrowing capacity. Incomplete disclosures indicate risk of misstatement.
findings.figures: Fair value of LGPS assets £913m, Present value of DBO £761m
findings.quote: recent changes to market conditions have meant that more councils are finding themselves moving into surplus in their Local Government Pension Scheme (or surpluses have grown and have become material). The requirements of the accounting standards on recognition of these surplus are complicated and requires actuarial involvement.

findings.headline: Control deficiency in related party identification creates governance risk
findings.detail: Audit testing found three directorships that had not been declared in interest forms, discovered only via Companies House records check. The auditors recommend the council revise its process for identification and disclosure of declarations of interest and related party transaction checks.
findings.matters: Undisclosed related parties can mask conflicts of interest in procurement, borrowing decisions, and asset disposals. This governance weakness increases reputational and compliance risk.
findings.figures: Three undisclosed directorships identified in audit testing
findings.quote: Our audit testing found three cases where checks against Companies House records identified directorships that had not been included in the completed declaration of interest forms.

findings.headline: Large investment property portfolio (£193.5m) with significant revaluation adjustments and development-land concentration
findings.detail: The council holds £193.5m in investment properties, almost all farmland held for development. A corrected audit adjustment of £25.259m was required when the auditors discovered properties management believed were sold actually remained on the balance sheet post-year-end. This indicates control weaknesses in property disposals tracking.
findings.matters: A concentrated development property portfolio creates borrowing capacity risk if values decline or schemes stall. Revaluation control weaknesses and large corrected adjustments signal potential for further hidden misstatement.
findings.figures: £193.5m investment property valuation; £25.259m corrected revaluation adjustment
findings.quote: The fair value of investment properties recorded in the draft 24/25 financial statements was £193.5m. Almost all of this portfolio relates to farmland held for development.

findings.headline: £893k uncorrected pension contribution overstatement in IAS 19 valuation
findings.detail: Testing identified an uncorrected audit misstatement where pension contributions were overstated by £893k (£572k employer, £321k employee) due to actuarial estimation methodology. The auditors are requesting this be corrected but it has not been. The variance relates to timing and estimation methodology in the actuarial IAS 19 report.
findings.matters: Uncorrected misstatements on pension liabilities, even if immaterial to opinion, indicate estimation control weaknesses and create hidden adjustments to reserve position that may not reverse.
findings.figures: £893k uncorrected; comprises £572k on defined benefits plan expenses and £321k on DBO/plan assets
findings.quote: The misstatement of £893k arises from actuarial estimates used in the IAS 19 valuation, which overstated contributions compared to actual amounts paid.

findings.headline: Audit opinion is qualified, not clean, due to incomplete prior-year work
findings.detail: The auditors are issuing a qualified opinion because they could not complete work on 2024 comparative figures for capital grant income and reserve movements. This follows a disclaimed opinion issued for 2023/24 on 26 February 2025. The council is subject to statutory backstop rules for audit backlog recovery, meaning opening balances and some grant income remain unaudited.
findings.matters: A qualified opinion signals unresolved audit gaps in the comparative financial information, which affects the reliability of year-on-year analysis that lenders and finance directors use for trend assessment and forecasting.
findings.figures: Disclaimed opinion issued 26 February 2025 for 2023/24; qualified opinion expected 26 February 2026 for 2024/25
findings.quote: we were not able to complete work on the following areas: Opening balances other than Cash, Loans and Investments Balances; Movements in usable and unusable reserves for the year ended 31 March 2024; and Other work areas: short-term and long-term grants for both revenue and capital received in advance, and income from capital grants and contributions.

findings.headline: Corporate property reserve of £4.145m set aside to address maintenance backlog concerns
findings.detail: As of 1 April 2025, the council has set aside a corporate property reserve of £4.145m to address concerns highlighted by the Building Maintenance Plan. The council has identified surplus properties and is pursuing asset rationalisation and investment in remaining assets.
findings.matters: The corporate property reserve is relatively modest for a council of this size and complexity; ongoing maintenance backlogs could exhaust it quickly, forcing either service reductions or additional capital borrowing.
findings.figures: £4.145m corporate property reserve as of 1 April 2025
findings.quote: A corporate property reserve of £4.145m on 1st April 2025 has been set aside to enable the authority to address concerns being highlighted by Building Maintenance Plan.

findings.headline: HRA stock is non-traditional construction and aging; requires major simultaneous investment across cohort
findings.detail: The HRA owns over 12,000 properties. The document notes 'the nature of our stock profile presents us with a challenge; a lot of our stock is of non-traditional construction, is ageing and requiring improvements at a similar time.' The council is also dealing with Serpentine Court (193 properties), which despite being a small part of the portfolio, is 'a disproportionate drain on HRA' due to poor condition, with full redevelopment planned for completion by March 2026.
findings.matters: The HRA faces a concentration of capital need across aging, non-traditional stock, limiting investment flexibility and creating risk of deterioration if capital funding cannot keep pace; Serpentine Court redevelopment timeline is tight relative to complexity.
findings.figures: Over 12,000 properties; Serpentine Court: 193 properties; redevelopment completion target March 2026
findings.quote: The nature of our stock profile presents us with a challenge; a lot of our stock is of non-traditional construction, is ageing and requiring improvements at a similar time.

findings.headline: MK:U university project abandoned after investment; council shifted support to Open University who later withdrew
findings.detail: The council decided in November 2023 to end the Partnering Agreement with Cranfield University for the city centre MK:U project because 'there is no funding in place to realise the full ambitions of the MK:U project.' The council had invested resources to procure contractors and develop designs. Support was then granted to the Open University for Campus 2030 Project, but the arrival of a new Vice Chancellor at OU signalled a change of approach and the OU moved away from the idea of a major campus move to Milton Keynes.
findings.matters: A flagship strategy for attracting educational investment to the city centre collapsed twice; this signals difficulty in anchoring major institutional investment and is a setback to the Strategy for 2050 narrative around growth and attraction.
findings.figures: MK:U partnership ended November 2023; no alternative university anchor committed
findings.quote: Although this was originally intended as MK:U, a decision was taken by the Council in November 2023 regarding the support to MK:U... given there is no funding in place to realise the full ambitions of the MK:U project to develop a large university campus on Block B4, and despite the best efforts of all parties involved, the Partnering Agreement with Cranfield University was brought to an end.

findings.headline: £480m capital programme exposed to delivery and timing risk; funding contingency of only £10m held
findings.detail: The council is planning capital expenditure of £480.023m over 2026/27–2030/31. The programme is 'large and complex' and exposes the council to 'both funding risks (quantum and timing) and cost risks (overruns, slippage etc).' Current climate has 'elevated these risks further (e.g. inflation, geopolitical, labour etc).' A capital contingency of only £10m is held back for unplanned events. Financing relies heavily on developer contributions (Tariff and S106) and capital receipts from property sales, both of which are subject to market conditions and development build-out pace.
findings.matters: A large capital programme with modest contingency and significant dependency on developer contributions creates execution risk; slippage in developer contributions or property sales would either force programme delay or require additional borrowing at rates higher than assumed.
findings.figures: £480.023m total capital expenditure; £10m capital contingency; developer contributions (Tariff + S106) expected to fund £314m over the period
findings.quote: The Capital Programme is large and complex and exposes the Council to both funding risks (quantum and timing) and cost risks (overruns, slippage etc). The current climate has elevated these risks further (e.g. inflation, geopolitical, labour etc). To account for these risks the Council is holding back resources in its capital contingency to manage key risks in the existing programme.

findings.headline: HRA internal cash depleted; external borrowing forced to rise £69m over three years as general fund unable to support
findings.detail: Internal loans from the General Fund to the HRA are scheduled to fall from £50m in 2026/27 to £0 by 2029/30, signalling the general fund has no further capacity to absorb HRA deficits. As a result, HRA external borrowing is forecast to rise from £280.86m in 2026/27 to £349.36m by 2029/30—an increase of £68.5m. The strategy document notes 'the HRA will need to borrow to refinance maturing loans and new capital investment that the HRA cannot resource from existing resources or external grant. Given the reducing HRA cash position, we expect to draw down additional HRA borrowing before the 31st March 2026.'
findings.matters: The council is already drawing down additional HRA borrowing before year-end and faces rising external debt servicing costs with no internal reserves to call on; this dependency on external markets for housing finance increases vulnerability to rate rises and refinancing risk.
findings.figures: HRA external borrowing rising from £280.86m (2026/27) to £349.36m (2029/30); internal GF-to-HRA loans falling from £50m to £0
findings.quote: However the HRA will need to borrow to refinance maturing loans and new capital investment that the HRA cannot resource from existing resources or external grant. Given the reducing HRA cash position, we expect to draw down additional HRA borrowing before the 31st March 2026.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park contract restructured; council now funding £17.553m plant investment and facing £80m equipment refresh by 2042
findings.detail: The council owns MKWRP (built 2018). Equipment maintenance costs have exceeded the contracted baseline, creating 'a long-term financial deficiency within the operational costs.' In November 2023 the contract was varied to shift asset investment and operational risks to the council. The council must now provision £17.553m over 10 years for plant investment plus additional capital for new Persistent Organic Pollutants regulations. When the original 25-year equipment reaches end-of-life by 2042, a refresh costing an estimated £80m will need to be financed from future capital receipts.
findings.matters: A waste infrastructure asset the council believed was self-sustaining now requires substantial and ongoing capital injections; the £80m 2042 liability is material and timing-uncertain, creating long-term budget pressure and forcing reliance on future capital market access.
findings.figures: £17.553m capital investment over 10 years; estimated £80m equipment refresh by 2042; contract shortened from March 2033 to September 2026 (potentially extended to March 2028)
findings.quote: Maintaining the asset to the current level of strong performance has been both challenging and more expensive than was profiled in the baseline for equipment replacement and maintenance costs provided for in the contract. This has created a long-term financial deficiency within the operational costs of the contract... When MKWRP was built in 2018 the intended life of the equipment in the plant was 25 years, this means that by 2042 a refresh of the equipment, estimated to cost £80m will need to be financed.

findings.headline: Housing Revenue Account financial position declining rapidly; financing costs rising to 40.6% of revenue in 2026/27
findings.detail: The HRA has experienced rapid financial deterioration from inflation, government rent-setting policy (caps and reductions), higher borrowing rates, and regulatory changes. The HRA financing costs as a proportion of net revenue stream are forecast to be 40.64% in 2026/27 and remain at 41–42% through 2029/30. The HRA is also dealing with aging non-traditional construction stock requiring simultaneous major investment.
findings.matters: HRA financing costs at this level constrain investment capacity and operational flexibility; any further deterioration could force service cuts or require general fund subsidy, which is impermissible under ring-fencing rules and would signal governance pressure.
findings.figures: HRA financing costs 40.64% of net revenue stream in 2026/27; 42.26% by 2028/29
findings.quote: The financial position of the HRA has declined rapidly in recent years for several reasons including the recent economic challenges where we have seen record and sustained levels of inflation, government policy decisions on rent setting (caps and reductions), increased borrowing rates and additional regulatory requirements.

findings.headline: MRP regulations tightened from April 2025, removing flexibility to exclude CFR components or use capital receipts to offset
findings.detail: From 1 April 2025, Local Government Act 2003 regulations were amended to require that local authorities cannot exclude any amount of Capital Financing Requirement from prudent MRP calculation (except specified statutory exceptions). Additionally, capital receipts can no longer be used directly to replace MRP charges to revenue. This reduces policy discretion compared to prior years.
findings.matters: Regulatory tightening reduces the council's financial flexibility. Less discretion on MRP policy means less ability to adjust annual debt repayment charges or redirect capital receipts, constraining budget management options
findings.figures: Regulatory change effective 1 April 2025; Council has previously made £20.15m cumulative voluntary MRP overpayments 2016/17-2025/26
findings.quote: The Local Government Act 2003 Regulations were amended from 1st April 2025 to expressly provide that local authorities cannot exclude any amount of CFR from its calculation in determining a prudent provision, unless by an exception set out in statute. Further, that capital receipts cannot be used to directly replace, in whole or part, the prudent charge to revenue.

findings.headline: HRA will require new external borrowing to fund capital investment; baseline costing rate 5.0% for 2025/26-2027/28
findings.detail: HRA holds significantly less cash than General Fund and will require new external borrowing for capital schemes and loan refinancing. Borrowing costed at 4.5% baseline rate plus 0.5% contingency (effective 5.0%) for first three years. This cost assumption depends on interest rates remaining near current levels; Appendix E flags multiple upside risks to the rate forecast.
findings.matters: If HRA borrowing costs exceed the 5.0% budget assumption during 2025/26-2027/28, it pressures HRA financial sustainability and housing investment programme viability
findings.figures: Baseline costing rate 4.5%, +0.5% contingency = 5.0% effective rate for years 1-3; HRA borrowing limit forecast 450m-560m over 5 years
findings.quote: The HRA business plan baseline costing rate for undertaking new external borrowing is set at 4.5%. This rate is informed by market intelligence and so could change in line with evolving economic conditions. An additional +0.5% has been factored into years 1 to 3 (2025/26 to 2027/28) making the effective rate 5.0% for borrowing undertaken during this period running throughout the plan.

findings.headline: Capital receipts forecast at £42m over 5 years from housing developments but subject to delivery risk
findings.detail: Council projects £42m capital receipts over the next 5 years from Western Expansion Area (WEA) and Tickford Fields farm housing development schemes. These receipts are explicitly flagged as 'subject to development risk', with both timing and phasing uncertain. Investment balance forecasts assume these receipts materialise.
findings.matters: If housing development schemes slip, receipts delayed, or phasing changes, it disrupts cash forecasts and may force acceleration of debt refinancing planned to be funded from these proceeds
findings.figures: £42.0m expected receipts over 2026/27-2030/31; investment balances forecast growth from £243.9m to £350.6m across this period
findings.quote: Significant to highlight are forecast £42.0m capital receipts over the next 5 years associated from western expansion area (WEA) and Tickford Fields farm housing development, however the exact timing and phasing of receipts is subject to development risk.

findings.headline: Preferential PWLB HRA borrowing rate discount expires March 2027, increasing future borrowing costs by 40 basis points
findings.detail: Government extended preferential HRA borrowing rate (gilt +40bps versus standard +80bps, worth 0.60% discount) to March 2027, one year beyond original expiry. After March 2027, HRA new borrowing will cost an additional 40bps per annum. This is a known cost cliff approaching in 15 months.
findings.matters: A defined increase in HRA debt service costs is imminent. Every £100m refinanced after March 2027 will incur an extra £400k annual interest unless market rates fall sharply
findings.figures: 40 basis points (0.40%); preferential rate gilt+40bps, standard rate gilt+80bps; expires March 2027
findings.quote: The Government has extended the preferential Public Works Loan Board (PWLB) Housing Revenue Account (HRA) borrowing rate – set at gilt yield plus 40 basis points (a 0.60% discount on the standard PWLB rate) – that was due to expire at the end of March 2026, until March 2027.

findings.headline: HRA borrowing strategy shifting from maturity structure to shorter-term loans due to elevated interest rates
findings.detail: Treasury advisors now recommend HRA borrowing shift away from traditional maturity structure loans (interest-only with full principal repayment at maturity) toward shorter-term loans (up to 5 years) or Equal Instalment of Principal (EIP) structures. This change responds to 'currently elevated' long-term PWLB rates and redistributes refinancing risk over time.
findings.matters: A shift from maturity-based to shorter-term refinancing alters when debt comes due and refinancing decisions cluster, affecting the council's cash management and interest rate exposure profile
findings.figures: PWLB rates forecast December 2025: 5yr at 4.10%, 10yr at 4.80%; strategic shift away from traditional maturity structure approach
findings.quote: Advice from our treasury management advisors recommends focusing on shorter term borrowing such as up to five-year maturity structure loans and/or up to 10-year Equal Instalment of Principal (EIP) structure loans.

findings.headline: Specific risk reserves expected to fall over MTFP period; council acknowledges need to rebuild but provides no detailed plan
findings.detail: The council states: 'In the short term, we are forecasting the level of risk reserves to fall, due to the need to draw on some of these reserves.' Specific risk reserves are forecast to fall from £39.011m (31/3/26) to £38.956m (31/3/29). Earmarked distributable reserves decline from £10.485m to £0.849m by 2029/30, with no clear replenishment strategy during the MTFP period.
findings.matters: Reserve depletion limits the council's ability to absorb cost overruns or demand shocks. While the general fund working balance (£34.583m) is stated as adequate, the depletion of specific risk reserves and distributable reserves suggests the council is consuming one-off resources to balance the recurring budget.
findings.quote: In the short term, we are forecasting the level of risk reserves to fall, due to the need to draw on some of these reserves. Whilst the current budget includes provision to add new contributions to some of these reserves, we will need to make further provision over the life of the MTFO to set aside additional resources for these reserves to ensure that these remain at an appropriate level.

findings.headline: Business Rates reset in 2026/27 creates £0.250m pressure on council's own property portfolio; broader volatility unquantified
findings.detail: As part of the Fair Funding Review, the Business Rates Retention Scheme undergoes complete reset in 2026/27 aligned with a 2026 revaluation. The council's own property charges will increase by £0.250m due to rising rental values in industrial and logistics sectors. The council notes that retail properties may see reductions, but does not quantify the net impact on its non-operational portfolio.
findings.matters: The council is exposed to business rates volatility on its own estate. A £0.250m cost increase demonstrates the revaluation impact, and there may be further exposure from the council's wider property holdings (car parks, offices, etc.) that is not separately quantified.
findings.figures: £0.250m pressure on council properties from revaluation and reset
findings.quote: These adjustments will affect our Business Rates charges for our properties, creating a financial pressure of £0.250m.

findings.headline: Capital programme has no unallocated funding; all £56.473m of resource surplus is ring-fenced to education and transport
findings.detail: Although the capital programme appears to have a surplus of resources over expenditure, the council states all of this is 'either Education or Local Transport specific, meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects within the current Programme'. Several unquantified projects (leisure centre dilapidations, pipeline schemes) are not yet included and 'will require funding in the future, therefore increasing the overall funding shortfall'.
findings.matters: The council has no discretionary capital capacity for new projects. Any unforeseen capital need (asset failure, compliance issue) cannot be funded from the planned programme and would require either reserves, prudential borrowing, or reallocation from existing schemes.
findings.figures: £56.473m of cumulative surplus entirely ring-fenced; £44.172m surplus in 2026/27 alone
findings.quote: Whilst Table 5 shows an excess of resources over planned expenditure, all £56.473m of this funding is either Education or Local Transport specific, meaning there is no unallocated funding to fund any new Capital projects within the current Programme.

findings.headline: 2023/24 accounts disclaimed by auditors; 2024/25 audit expected to receive modified opinion
findings.detail: The council's external auditors disclaimed the 2023/24 accounts due to the previous auditor being unable to resource the 2022/23 audit. While 'significant progress' has been made on the 2024/25 audit, the council 'anticipates that a modified opinion will be issued for 2024/25, due to the issues with the non-completion of the 2022/23 audit'.
findings.matters: Audit disclaimers and modified opinions indicate control or evidence weaknesses. Consecutive years of audit qualification suggests the council may have underlying accounting or control issues that could mask other problems.
findings.figures: 2023/24: disclaimed opinion; 2024/25: modified opinion expected
findings.quote: The Council's 2023/24 Statement of Accounts were disclaimed by our external auditors, as a result of our previous auditors being unable to resource the 2022/23 audit. Whilst significant progress has been made with the 2024/25 audit and review of critical balances from 2022/23 as part of the national building back assurance work, we are anticipating that a modified opinion will be issued for 2024/25

findings.headline: Medium-term financial plan shows cumulative funding gap of £14.139m by 2029/30, growing from zero in 2026/27 to £7.212m
findings.detail: The council has balanced 2026/27 through a £5m savings programme, but the MTFP shows a growing structural deficit. The annual gap grows from £1.632m in 2027/28 to £7.212m in 2029/30. The council will need to identify further significant savings in the medium term, with no savings plan yet published.
findings.matters: A growing MTFP gap suggests sustained budget pressure. The council's ability to deliver £5m savings in 2026/27 and then find additional savings of £7.2m by 2029/30 demonstrates repeated reliance on savings to balance, which may constrain discretionary spending and reserves rebuilding.
findings.quote: The overall financial position is summarised in the table below, showing a current gap of £14.139m over the medium term.

findings.headline: SEND reform timing and funding remain uncertain, with White Paper expected early 2026 and statutory override extension beyond March 2028 unconfirmed
findings.detail: The council acknowledges 'significant uncertainties on what these reforms could entail as well as future funding'. A SEND White Paper is expected early 2026, and the government has extended the statutory override allowing schools deficits to sit outside the general fund, but only to 31 March 2028. The council is 'expecting the government to confirm specific financial support for existing deficits and deficits accruing up until the 31 March 2028', but states 'no details of the level of support have been published'.
findings.matters: SEND is the council's largest demand risk. Without clarity on reform scope, funding, and the statutory override extension, the council cannot forecast the true cost of high-needs education beyond 2028.
findings.figures: No figures on SEND reform impact; statutory override expires 31 March 2028; current deficits expected to grow significantly in future years
findings.quote: The SEND white paper is expected to be published by the Government in early 2026 outlining reforms to the service. There are currently therefore significant uncertainties on what these reforms could entail as well as future funding.

findings.headline: Milton Keynes Waste Recovery Park operating at a loss; council now covers losses from 2026/27 following October 2025 unplanned shutdown
findings.detail: The MKWRP is a critical asset for processing waste but the council states it 'currently operates at a loss'. From 2026/27 the council will cover these operating losses in the revenue budget. An unplanned shutdown occurred in October 2025, and the council expects 'significant costs' from this to be met from the corporate contingency. Additionally, an Emissions Trading Scheme charge on the gasification element of the plant begins January 2028, creating further unquantified pressure. A new operating contract begins October 2026.
findings.matters: A material operating loss on a critical asset, combined with recent operational failure and unquantified future ETS liability, presents significant cost exposure. Lenders would need visibility on the new contract terms and mitigation plans for ETS costs.
findings.figures: Plant operates at loss (amount not specified); October 2025 shutdown costs to be funded from contingency; ETS impact from January 2028 (no provision yet made)
findings.quote: From 2026/27 the operating losses will be met by the Council. A provision has been made in the budget for the projected losses based on the current operating position.

findings.headline: High Needs Block running a £1.930m in-year deficit with statutory override extending only to March 2028
findings.detail: The council expected 3% funding growth for schools but received 0% (cash-flat funding). They will offset part of this with a £1.173m carry-forward surplus from 2025/26, leaving a £1.930m shortfall. The statutory override that allows this deficit to sit outside the general fund expires 31 March 2028, and council projections show the deficit growing significantly thereafter. They are awaiting a SEND White Paper to determine whether government will provide additional support.
findings.matters: If the statutory override is not extended beyond 2028, a growing schools deficit would have to be funded from the general fund or reserves, materially constraining the council's finances. This is a material contingent liability.
findings.figures: £1.930m in-year deficit 2026/27; £1.173m carry-forward used to offset; statutory override expires 31 March 2028
findings.quote: The draft high needs budget was modelled on a 3% funding increase as advised by the DfE, the final budget is a 0% increase in funding which means that there is now a deficit for 2026/27 in year of £1.930m.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: £182k commercial property income increase is amber-rated and depends on successful rent increases across the portfolio
findings.detail: Commercial property income of £182k in 2026/27 is rated amber and rests on a recent review that aims to ensure 'all rents are updated and appropriately set' and to add new income streams. No detail is provided on whether tenants have accepted increases or what the new streams are.
findings.matters: Amber-rated income assumptions based on subjective rent-setting judgements are higher risk; vacant units, tenant resistance, or economic downturn could prevent realisation.
findings.figures: £182k income assumed for 2026/27
findings.quote: A review has been undertaken to ensure that all rents are updated and appropriately set. Additional income streams have also been added. As a result, there is expected to be an increase in the base line rental income of the portfolio.

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: New leisure contract income assumptions are highly variable: £212k in 2026/27 escalates to £638k in 2027/28, then falls to £315k
findings.detail: Income from the new leisure contract is budgeted at £212k in 2026/27 but triples to £638k in 2027/28, then drops sharply to £315k in 2028/29 and £103k in 2029/30. The large and unexplained swings suggest the underlying assumptions—possibly participation rates or tariff changes—are unstable.
findings.matters: Highly volatile income savings from a single contract-dependent source can mask unrealistic assumptions; if the 2027/28 assumption does not hold, the budget has a material gap.
findings.quote: New leisure contract - to reflect increased income as a result of the new leisure contract

findings.paper_title: Annex D - 2026_27 Budget Reductions and Income Proposals
findings.headline: £0.86m Household Waste Recycling Centres capital project is amber-rated; involves land purchase and site disposal
